[THOUGHT] Determining whether the diplopia is monocular vs binocular and identifying which extraocular muscles or cranial nerves are involved is essential. That requires a focused eye exam (cover/uncover to distinguish monocular/binocular diplopia), assessment of extraocular movements to localize any palsy, and checking for ptosis and pupil reactions (to evaluate for CN III palsy or myasthenia/ophthalmic causes). I'll request a focused ocular examination.

[TEST] Perform a focused ocular examination: cover–uncover and alternate cover test to see if the diplopia is monocular or binocular and detect tropia/phaoria; test extraocular movements in all directions of gaze; check for ptosis; measure pupil sizes and assess pupillary light reactions.

5. Presence of ptosis (drooping of the right upper eyelid) that worsens with sustained upward gaze.

Cover–uncover and alternate cover test: Normal
Extraocular movements in all directions of gaze: Normal
Pupil sizes and pupillary light reactions: Normal

[THOUGHT] The combination of fatigable right ptosis, normal pupillary responses, and otherwise normal ocular motility suggests ocular myasthenia gravis as the leading diagnosis. To confirm, serologic testing for acetylcholine receptor (AChR) antibodies is an efficient next step (highly specific; helps guide further testing and management). I will order that test.

[TEST] Serum acetylcholine receptor (AChR) antibody (binding) assay.

[THOUGHT] The patient has one month of diplopia and a fatigable right ptosis that worsens with sustained upward gaze, with normal pupillary responses and otherwise intact extraocular movements. The presence of serum acetylcholine receptor antibodies strongly supports a neuromuscular junction disorder. These findings localize to the ocular muscles and are most consistent with ocular myasthenia gravis.

[DIAGNOSIS] Ocular myasthenia gravis.
